items.stem: A function passes all its tests with your 5 test students. In production, with 5,000 enrollments, the page takes 30 seconds to load. Which kind of defect is most likely?

options.text: A query that runs once for every row, which only becomes slow with real data.
options.feedback: This is the N+1 problem. Five rows cost six queries and nobody notices. Five thousand rows cost five thousand and one.

options.text: A typing mistake in a variable name.
options.feedback: A typing mistake would fail on the first run, including with 5 students.

options.text: A method that does not exist.
options.feedback: A missing method fails with an error the first time the code runs.

options.text: Two requests overlapping.
options.feedback: An overlap produces wrong data once in a while. It does not make every page load slow.

items.stem: Of the four snippets, the one that calls the invented method get_or_none() is the easiest to catch. Why?

options.text: It fails with an error the first time you run it. The other three run without any error.
options.feedback: A missing method stops the program at once. The other defects produce results that look normal.

options.text: Reviewers recognize fake methods at a glance.
options.feedback: The method looks real. It fits the style of the others, which is why a reader can miss it.

options.text: It is the only one that has a test.
options.feedback: Tests are not the difference. A test that never runs the line would not catch it either.

options.text: It is the only one that changes the database.
options.feedback: The close-a-course snippet changes the database too, and it runs without error.

items.stem: A student describes a landing page to a model, pastes the result into a browser, and asks for changes until it looks right. The student never reads the code. Which term fits best?

options.text: Vibe coding.
options.feedback: The student judges the result by whether it seems to work. For a throwaway page, that is a reasonable approach.

options.text: Agentic coding.
options.feedback: Agentic coding means the AI has a shell, your repository and your tests, and acts on them in a loop. Here the student does the running and pasting.

options.text: Code review.
options.feedback: Review means reading the code with a checklist. The student does not read it.

options.text: Neither, because AI wrote the code.
options.feedback: Both terms describe code written with AI. They differ in how the work is done.

items.stem: Why can agentic coding do more damage without being asked than a chat that only suggests code?

options.text: The agent can run commands and change files by itself, so a wrong decision takes effect at once.
options.feedback: A suggestion does nothing until you use it. An agent acts, and its actions can include deleting or overwriting files.

options.text: Agents are built on models that make more mistakes.
options.feedback: The model can be the same. The difference is what the model is allowed to do.

options.text: Agents write longer code, and long code has more bugs.
options.feedback: Length is not the main risk. The risk is that the agent acts without your reading each step.

options.text: Agents ignore your test suite.
options.feedback: Agents usually run the tests. The tests can still miss a defect, as the snippets show.

items.stem: You are watching an agent work on a project. Which of these are worth writing down? Select all that apply.

options.text: A confident claim that turned out to be wrong.
options.feedback: This shows how a plausible answer can be wrong, and how you found out.

options.text: A moment when it changed course after an Observation, such as a failing test.
options.feedback: This shows what outside information corrected it, and how many steps it had built on the wrong answer.

options.text: A change it made that nobody asked for.
options.feedback: Unrequested changes add review work and can hide new problems.

options.text: How fast it typed.
options.feedback: Speed does not tell you whether the work can be trusted.
